Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 75, verse 1–4:

(﴿I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ ﴿Nor do I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾ ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ ﴿Yes! We are able to restore even his fingertips﴾

The opening of the surah with an oath signals that what follows is a matter of great importance, so that the listener's soul becomes attentive to it, as has been mentioned in several places concerning the oaths of the Qur'an.

That the oath is sworn by the Day of Resurrection is an excellent opening (bara'at istihlal), because the purpose of the surah is to describe the Day of Resurrection.

Also in it is that the one sworn by is the same as the matter sworn about, to indicate the increase of its status in the eyes of the one swearing, as in the words of Abu Tammam:

"Your front teeth, indeed they are a bud of pearls, and the pearls are uniform, and a flash and a glimmer."

As has been mentioned in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He (﴿Ha Mim. By the Clear Book. Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 1–3]) in Surat al-Zukhruf.

The formula "I do not swear" is a formula of oath, in which the negative particle has been placed upon the verb "aqsama" (I swear), for the purpose of emphasizing the sanctity of the one sworn by, to the extent that it gives the listener the impression that the speaker intends to swear by it and then refrains from swearing out of fear of breaking the oath by it. So he says: "I do not swear by it", meaning: nor do I swear by anything more honored than it in my estimation. This is a metonymy for the emphasis of the oath. It has been mentioned in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He (﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 75]) in Surat al-Waqi'a.

In it is also a rhetorical embellishment of the kind called "affirming praise by what resembles blame" (ta'kid al-madh bi-ma yushbih al-dham). We have not mentioned this in what preceded, and no one has mentioned it.

The oath "by the Day of Resurrection" is understood as a time-frame for what takes place in it of God's justice, the outpouring of His grace, and what is present in it of the angels and the blessed souls.

The discussion of "the Day of Resurrection" has preceded more than once, among them His saying, exalted is He (﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment﴾ [al-Baqara: 85]) in Surat al-Baqara.

The answer to the oath is understood from His saying (﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾), because it is the indicator of the answer, since the estimate is: "We will certainly assemble the bones of man. Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?"

In the Kashshaf: "They said that it (i.e., 'la uqsimu') in the Imam is without an alif, and he disavowed it with the expression 'they said', because it contradicts what is found in the codices (masahif)." It has been attributed to al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, that he read "la-uqsimu" (with a lam) the first time without an alif, and this is a transmission from him mentioned by Shaykh 'Ali al-Nuri in Ghayth al-Naf', but al-Shatibi did not mention it. Ibn 'Atiyya limited himself to attributing it to Ibn Kathir without qualification, so the lam is then the lam of oath. The well-known position from Ibn Kathir is otherwise. He placed the phrase "wa la uqsimu" as an emphasis on the clause to which it is conjoined. The definiteness of "al-nafs" is the definiteness of the genus, i.e., the self-reproaching souls. The intended meaning is the souls of the believers. The description "al-lawwama" is an intensive form, because it greatly reproaches its owner for shortcoming in piety and obedience. This reproach is what is termed in technical usage "accountability", and its reproach occurs through its thinking and inner speech. Al-Hasan said: "The believer is not seen except that he blames himself for what has passed and regrets it. He blames himself for evil, why he did it, and for good, why he did not increase it. These are truly good souls, worthy to be honored by swearing by them, and the Day of Resurrection was only for their honor."

The intended meaning is the self that reproaches in this world, a reproach from which repentance and piety arise; the intended meaning is not the reproach of the Hereafter, when it says (﴿O, would that I had sent forth for my life﴾ [al-Fajr: 24]).

The connection of the oath by them with the Day of Resurrection is that they are the souls that attain success on that day. It is related from some exegetes that "la uqsimu" is meant to express non-swearing, so they explained "the self-reproaching soul" as the one that reproaches for not doing good.

His saying (﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾) etc. is evidence for the answer to the oath, since the estimate of the answer is: "We will certainly assemble your bones and raise you for reckoning."

The definiteness of "al-insan" is the definiteness of the genus, and its occurrence in the context of denial, which is in the sense of negation, requires generality. It is a customary generality, considered with regard to the majority of people at that time, since the believers were few. So the meaning is: "Does the disbelieving man think...?"

The clause (﴿that We will not assemble his bones﴾) is composed of the particle "an" with a open hamza and a light nun, which is the sister of "inna" with a kasra.

The subject of "an" is a omitted pronoun of the matter (damir al-shan).

The clause after "an" is a predicate of the pronoun of the matter. Sibawayh makes "an" with its subject and predicate fill the place of the two objects of the verb of opinion. Al-Akhfash makes "an" with its two parts in the position of the first object, that is, because it is a verbal noun, and posits a second object. This is because among the special properties of verbs of the heart is that the open-hamzated "an" may enter after them, so the verb is satisfied by "an" with its subject and predicate from its two objects.

The particle "lan", which indicates the emphasis of negation, is used to convey the belief of the polytheists in the impossibility of assembling bones after they have decayed and scattered.

Al-Qurtubi said: It was revealed concerning 'Adi ibn Rabi'a (the correct is Ibn Abi Rabi'a) who said to the Prophet ﷺ: "O Muhammad, tell me about the Day of Resurrection." The Messenger of God ﷺ informed him, and 'Adi said: "If I witnessed that day, I would not believe you, or that God would gather the bones." So this verse was revealed. Did you not say: the cause of revelation does not restrict the statement to this questioner?

The bones: a metonymy for the whole body, and they were singled out for mention to convey their sayings: (﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya Sin: 78]) (﴿When we are bones and crumbled remains, shall we indeed be resurrected?﴾ [al-Isra': 49]) (﴿When we are decayed bones?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 11]). They argued by the impossibility of the bones accepting re-creation after decay, so that the impossibility of re-creating the flesh, sinew and heart is a fortiori. Thus the affirmation of the re-creation of the bones implies that the re-creation of the rest of the body is equal to that of the bone, and in this there is sufficient proof with brevity.

Then, if the re-creation is by gathering the parts of their bodies scattered as atoms, which God knows, and this is one of the two positions of our scholars, then the verb "najma'a" is taken in its literal sense. If the resurrection is by creating other bodies in the forms of the perishing bodies, whether as a new creation or as a beginning from the remnant of the tailbone (a'jab al-adhnab), as occurs in some reports, and these are two positions of our scholars, then the verb "najma'a" is used metaphorically for the creation which is in the form of the body that decayed. The reason for this metaphorical use is the agreement (mushakala) with the sayings of the polytheists which are intended to be refuted, to avoid entering with them into describing the manner of resurrection. For this reason you do not find in the verses of the Qur'an except their general outline, and therefore the scholars of Islam differed concerning the manner of re-creating bodies at the resurrection. Imam al-Haramayn chose to suspend judgment, and the verses of the Qur'an contain what suits both matters.

"Bala" is a particle that cancels the negation indicated by "lan najma'a 'izamahu", so its meaning is: "Rather, his bones will be gathered," according to the difference of the two interpretations of the meaning of gathering.

"Qadirin" is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in the omitted verb after "bala", which is indicated by His saying "an lan najma'a", i.e., "Rather, We will gather them while We are able to restore even his fingertips."

It is also possible that "bala" is a cancellation of the two negations: the negation conveyed by the interrogative of denial in His saying "Does man think", and the negation within the object of "yahsabu", and this is a cancellation by rebuke, i.e., "Rather, let him think us able," because the import of "an lan najma'a 'izamahu" is that we are not able to gather his bones, so "qadirin" is a second object of the supposed "yahsibna". He changed the complement of "qadirin" from saying "able to gather his bones" to "able to restore even his fingertips", because it is richer in meaning and more suited to the intention of summarizing the manner of resurrection and re-creation.

In observance of these meanings, the reading "qadirun" with a nominative was avoided, with the estimate "we are able", so it was not read with the nominative.

The "taswiya" is the straightening of a thing and the perfecting of creation. God, exalted is He, said (﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ [al-Shams: 7]), and He said in this surah (﴿So He created and proportioned﴾ [al-Qiyama: 38]). By "taswiya" is meant the re-creation of the fingertips shaped and perfected, so "taswiya" is a metonymy for creation, because it entails it, for nothing is proportioned except that its creation has been renewed. God, exalted is He, said (﴿He who created and proportioned﴾ [al-A'la: 2]).

"Al-Banan" is the fingers of the two hands and the two feet, or the tips of those fingers. It is a collective noun of "banana".

Since they are the smallest of the members situated at the extremity of the body, their proportioning is a metonymy for the proportioning of the whole body, since it is evident that the proportioning of the extremities of the body requires the proportioning of what is before them, as you say: "The wind uprooted the tent's pegs," meaning it uprooted the whole tent, for an extremity of a thing may be used as a metonymy for the whole of it.

From this is their saying: "This thing is yours in its entirety" (bi-asrihi), meaning with the rope with which it is tied, as a metonymy for the whole thing. Likewise their saying: "It is yours with its whole rope" (bi-rummatihi), meaning with the cord with which it is bound.

"Bala" is a particle that cancels the negation indicated by "lan najma'a 'izamahu", so its meaning is: "Rather, his bones will be gathered," according to the difference of the two interpretations of the meaning of gathering.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 75, verse 1–4:

(﴿I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ ﴿Nor do I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾ ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ ﴿Yes! We are able to restore even his fingertips﴾

The opening of the surah with an oath signals that what follows is a matter of great importance, so that the listener's soul becomes attentive to it, as has been mentioned in several places concerning the oaths of the Qur'an.

That the oath is sworn by the Day of Resurrection is an excellent opening (bara'at istihlal), because the purpose of the surah is to describe the Day of Resurrection.

Also in it is that the one sworn by is the same as the matter sworn about, to indicate the increase of its status in the eyes of the one swearing, as in the words of Abu Tammam:

"Your front teeth, indeed they are a bud of pearls, and the pearls are uniform, and a flash and a glimmer."

As has been mentioned in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He (﴿Ha Mim. By the Clear Book. Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 1–3]) in Surat al-Zukhruf.

The formula "I do not swear" is a formula of oath, in which the negative particle has been placed upon the verb "aqsama" (I swear), for the purpose of emphasizing the sanctity of the one sworn by, to the extent that it gives the listener the impression that the speaker intends to swear by it and then refrains from swearing out of fear of breaking the oath by it. So he says: "I do not swear by it", meaning: nor do I swear by anything more honored than it in my estimation. This is a metonymy for the emphasis of the oath. It has been mentioned in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He (﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 75]) in Surat al-Waqi'a.

In it is also a rhetorical embellishment of the kind called "affirming praise by what resembles blame" (ta'kid al-madh bi-ma yushbih al-dham). We have not mentioned this in what preceded, and no one has mentioned it.

The oath "by the Day of Resurrection" is understood as a time-frame for what takes place in it of God's justice, the outpouring of His grace, and what is present in it of the angels and the blessed souls.

The discussion of "the Day of Resurrection" has preceded more than once, among them His saying, exalted is He (﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment﴾ [al-Baqara: 85]) in Surat al-Baqara.

The answer to the oath is understood from His saying (﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾), because it is the indicator of the answer, since the estimate is: "We will certainly assemble the bones of man. Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?"

In the Kashshaf: "They said that it (i.e., 'la uqsimu') in the Imam is without an alif, and he disavowed it with the expression 'they said', because it contradicts what is found in the codices (masahif)." It has been attributed to al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, that he read "la-uqsimu" (with a lam) the first time without an alif, and this is a transmission from him mentioned by Shaykh 'Ali al-Nuri in Ghayth al-Naf', but al-Shatibi did not mention it. Ibn 'Atiyya limited himself to attributing it to Ibn Kathir without qualification, so the lam is then the lam of oath. The well-known position from Ibn Kathir is otherwise. He placed the phrase "wa la uqsimu" as an emphasis on the clause to which it is conjoined. The definiteness of "al-nafs" is the definiteness of the genus, i.e., the self-reproaching souls. The intended meaning is the souls of the believers. The description "al-lawwama" is an intensive form, because it greatly reproaches its owner for shortcoming in piety and obedience. This reproach is what is termed in technical usage "accountability", and its reproach occurs through its thinking and inner speech. Al-Hasan said: "The believer is not seen except that he blames himself for what has passed and regrets it. He blames himself for evil, why he did it, and for good, why he did not increase it. These are truly good souls, worthy to be honored by swearing by them, and the Day of Resurrection was only for their honor."

The intended meaning is the self that reproaches in this world, a reproach from which repentance and piety arise; the intended meaning is not the reproach of the Hereafter, when it says (﴿O, would that I had sent forth for my life﴾ [al-Fajr: 24]).

The connection of the oath by them with the Day of Resurrection is that they are the souls that attain success on that day. It is related from some exegetes that "la uqsimu" is meant to express non-swearing, so they explained "the self-reproaching soul" as the one that reproaches for not doing good.

His saying (﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾) etc. is evidence for the answer to the oath, since the estimate of the answer is: "We will certainly assemble your bones and raise you for reckoning."

The definiteness of "al-insan" is the definiteness of the genus, and its occurrence in the context of denial, which is in the sense of negation, requires generality. It is a customary generality, considered with regard to the majority of people at that time, since the believers were few. So the meaning is: "Does the disbelieving man think...?"

The clause (﴿that We will not assemble his bones﴾) is composed of the particle "an" with a open hamza and a light nun, which is the sister of "inna" with a kasra.

The subject of "an" is a omitted pronoun of the matter (damir al-shan).

The clause after "an" is a predicate of the pronoun of the matter. Sibawayh makes "an" with its subject and predicate fill the place of the two objects of the verb of opinion. Al-Akhfash makes "an" with its two parts in the position of the first object, that is, because it is a verbal noun, and posits a second object. This is because among the special properties of verbs of the heart is that the open-hamzated "an" may enter after them, so the verb is satisfied by "an" with its subject and predicate from its two objects.

The particle "lan", which indicates the emphasis of negation, is used to convey the belief of the polytheists in the impossibility of assembling bones after they have decayed and scattered.

Did you not say: the cause of revelation does not restrict the statement to this questioner?

Nay, [﴿man wishes to continue in sin ahead of him﴾]. *Bal* ("nay") marks a transitional disengagement (*idrab intiqali*) to mention another aspect of their immorality. So the sentence after *bal* stands as a resumptive new sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*), because of the connection between the two sentences. That is, when they were called to abandon polytheism and what it entails of sins, and were warned of the punishment for it on the Day of Resurrection, they were determined to persist in disbelief.

*Al-fujur* (immorality, grave wrongdoing) means severe evil conduct, and it is also used for lying. From this, a false oath is described as *fajira*. So *fajara* can mean *kadhaba* ("he lied") in both form and meaning, and it can be intransitive or transitive, like the verb *kadhaba*. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said, "that is, the disbeliever denies what is ahead of him." It is also related from Ibn Qutaybah that a Bedouin asked 'Umar ibn al-Khattab to carry him on a mount, and complained of the rear of his mount. 'Umar suspected him, so the Bedouin said:

*Its back was not harmed by any wound or sore,*
*Abu Hafs 'Umar swore by God.*
*So forgive him, O God, if he has lied.*

He said: that is, if he attributed lying to me.

His words [﴿man wishes﴾] may be a report about what is in the souls of the people of polytheism, of their love for continuing in the transgression and immorality they are engaged in.

It may also be a rhetorical interrogative (*istifham inkari*) consistent with the context of what precedes it, his words [﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ (75:3)].

The word *al-insan* (man) is repeated for emphasis (*izhar fi maqam al-idmar*), because the context calls for reproach and for marvelling at his error.

The word *al-insan* is repeated five times in this surah for this purpose, with the added specificity that its repetition the second time and the fourth and fifth times makes each of those three clauses in which it occurs independent in meaning.

The *lam* in His words *li-yafjura* is the *lam* that frequently occurs after the verbs *amara* ("to command") and *arada* ("to wish"), as in [﴿I have been commanded to act justly among you﴾ (42:15)], [﴿Allah wishes to make clear to you﴾ (4:26)], and the verse of Kuthayyir:

*I wish to forget her love, but it is as if Layla appears to me in every place.*

The verb after it is in the subjunctive governed by an implied *an* ("that"), because this *lam* is originally the *lam* of purpose (*lam al-ta'lil*). For this reason it is said to be the *lam* of purpose, and it is also said to be extra (*za'ida*). It is narrated from Sibawayh that the verb preceding this *lam* is taken as a masdar in the nominative, as the subject, and the *lam* and what follows it are its predicate, meaning their wish for immorality. They agree that the verb following it has no object, because of this special usage of it. Al-Nahhas said: some reciters named it *lam an* (the *lam* of *an*). Its discussion has been covered in several places, including at His words [﴿Allah wishes to make clear to you﴾ (4:26)] in Surat al-Nisa'.

*Amam* (ahead, in front of): its original meaning is a noun for the place opposite to whatever it is attached to. It is the opposite of *khalf* (behind). It is used figuratively for future time. Ibn 'Abbas said: he denies the Day of Reckoning. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: he denies what is ahead of him, *safat* (a single note of contempt or a vague reference to the future).

The pronoun in *amamahu* may refer to *al-insan*, meaning in his future, that is, in the remainder of his life. He thus proceeds forward, driving on headlong, not refraining from the immorality he is in. He denies resurrection, so he does not restrain himself from the immorality he does not wish to restrain. Ibn 'Abbas and his companions adopted this meaning.

*Amamahu* may also refer to the future day, used figuratively. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas in one narration, and of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd. In that case *yafjura* means *yukadhdhibu* ("denies"), that is, he denies the future day.

( ﴿He asks: when is the Day of Resurrection?﴾

This sentence may be connected to the one before it, as a *badal ishtimal* (a substitute by inclusion, i.e. a substitute that is related to its antecedent by containing or implying it), since his intent to persist in wickedness includes mockery of the Day of Resurrection. It may also be a *badal mutabiq* (a substitute that corresponds exactly to its antecedent), according to the interpretation of ﴿He lets wickedness loose before him﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 5] as denial of the Day of Resurrection.

It may also be a *musta'nafa* (a resumptive, independent sentence), expressing wonder at the state of their question about the time of the Day of Resurrection. It is a question asked in mockery, because they believe its occurrence to be impossible.

*Ayyan* (أيّانَ) is an interrogative particle asking about a distant time, because its original form is *ayyu an kadha* (i.e. "which time is this"). For this reason it is found in some Arabic dialects with a damma on the *nun*. In the standard language they used a fatha on the *nun*, because they treated the whole word as an adverb of time, so that *ayyan* came to mean *mata* (when). This was discussed previously at His words, exalted is He, ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive?﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], in al-A'raf. The meaning is that they ask for the specifying of a known, fixed time, after years and the like, or for that which would specify it for the questioners, such as an event that would coincide with this day. Thus it is a request to determine a term for the arrival of a day on which people will rise.

[Page 344]

It was diverted from answering by specifying a time for the Day of Resurrection to warning them of its terrors, because they were not sincere in their question. Therefore, given their condition, it was appropriate that they be warned of the terrors that will occur at the arrival of this day, together with an affirmation of its certain occurrence. The words of the Qur'an are guidance and direction, and they leave no opportunity for guidance and direction without seizing it. This is a warning from its beginning, which came in the form of specifying the time of the Day of Resurrection, creating the impression of an answer to their question, as if their words were being taken in a sense other than mockery, by way of what is called the wise method of address (al-uslub al-hakim, a rhetorical approach of responding to a question in a manner other than its literal intent in order to guide the questioner). In it there is also an indirect rebuke, for they had been negligent in guarding against that day and had busied themselves with asking about its time. Close to this is what is reported: that a man from among the Muslims asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "When is the Hour?" He said to him: "What have you prepared for it?"

These states mentioned in the verse are among what occurs at the arrival of the Hour and the rising of the Resurrection, so this was a form of specifying its time through specifying its signs.

The fa' (the particle "then") is for the consequence of the answer to the question.

The word (بَرِقَ) was read by the majority with a kasra on the rā', and its meaning is: he was dazed and bewildered. It is said: "baraqa yabraqu, fa-huwa bariq", from the pattern of faraha, and it is thus one of the states of a human being.

In the verse, it is ascribed to the sight (al-basar) by way of the rational metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli, a figure in which an action is ascribed to something other than its real agent), placing it in the position of the place of dazzlement, because when a person is bewildered, his gaze becomes fixed. Likewise, al-A'sha ascribed dazzlement to the eyes in his saying:

"Thus do, as long as you live, when they scatter (in war), and advance when the eyes of people are wide-staring (in fear)."

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read it with a fatha on the rā', from al-bariq, meaning glittering: that is, the sight glittered from the intensity of its fixed staring, and its present tense is yabruqu with a damma on the rā'. Its ascription to the sight is literal.

The meaning of the two readings is one, and it is a metonymy (al-kinaya, an expression in which the intended meaning is conveyed indirectly) for fear and terror, like His, exalted is He: ﴿And the true promise draws near, and behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved stare fixedly﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:97]. So there is no basis for al-Tabari's preference for the reading of the majority over the reading of Nafi' and Abu Ja'far, neither from the standpoint of the wording, nor of the meaning, nor of what the interpretation requires.

The definite article in (al-basar) is for the genus, intended to be comprehensive (al-istighraq), meaning the sights of all people, from the severity that occurs at that time, while they differ in the terror that befalls them according to their differing positions in the ways of their stations.

[Page 345]

The eclipse of the moon is meant to refer to the extinguishing of its light in a continuous extinction, due to its being shaken from its orbit around the earth, which revolves around the sun, such that its light is not reflected upon it and it does not appear luminous to people. This is what His saying indicates: ﴿and the sun and the moon are joined together﴾. Thus this eclipse is not its usual eclipse, which occurs when the earth comes between the moon and its alignment with the sun.

The meaning of the joining of the sun and the moon is the moon's adhering to the sun, so the sun swallows it, because the moon is detached from the earth, which is among the bodies revolving around the sun like the planets. This will be due to a disruption of the gravitational force by which God established the solar system.

The phrase (when the sight is dazzled) is a temporal clause (zarf) related to (﴿the human being will say﴾). It was placed before its governing element for the sake of emphasizing the temporal clause, because it is the focus of the context of the reply to His saying: ﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:6].

The explicit statement that this is the arrival of the Day of Resurrection is omitted, being sufficient with mention of what indicates it, namely their saying: ﴿Where is the escape?﴾. It is as if it were said: the Day of Resurrection has arrived and its terrors have come, the human being will say on that day. Then it was emphasized by His saying: ﴿To your Lord on that day is the place of rest﴾.

(يَوْمَئِذٍ, "on that day") is also a temporal clause related to (yaqulu, "he will say"), meaning: the day when the sight is dazzled, the moon is eclipsed, and the sun and moon are joined. The tanwin on (إذْ, "when") is the compensatory tanwin (tanwin al-'iwad, the nunation that replaces an omitted element) in place of the omitted clause, which is indicated by the clause to which (إذْ) is annexed.

(يَوْمَئِذٍ) was mentioned even though His saying (إذا بَرَقَ البَصَرُ, "when the sight is dazzled") and what follows already implies it, for the sake of emphasis on mentioning that day, which they used to deny the occurrence of and mock, asking about its time. It also serves to make clear that these three states occur at one and the same time.

The human being (al-insan) is the one spoken of in His saying: ﴿Does the human being think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:3]. That is, the disbelieving human being will say on that day: "Where is the escape?"

(al-mafarr, "the escape"), with a fatha on the mim and a fatha on the fa', is a verbal noun (masdar). The interrogative is used in the sense of wishing (tamanni), meaning: "Would that I had an escape to a place of safety," but he is not able to attain it.

(أيْنَ, "where") is an adverb of place.

(kalla, "no!") is a repudiation and nullification of what was contained in ﴿Where is the escape?﴾ of the hope of finding a way of escape.

[Page 346]

(al-wazar) is the place to which one takes refuge to protect oneself from being struck by something disagreeable, such as mountains and fortresses.

It is possible that ﴿No! There is no refuge﴾ is a new statement from the side of Allah, exalted is He, as an answer to the human being's utterance, meaning: there is no refuge for you. In that case, it is proper to pause at (al-mafarr). It is also possible that it is part of the human being's utterance, meaning: he says, "Where is the escape?" and answers himself by nullifying his hope, saying ﴿No! There is no refuge﴾, meaning: there is no refuge for me. This is by his looking in all directions and finding nothing but the Fire, as is reported in the hadith. In that case, it is good to connect (﴿Where is the escape?﴾) with the clause (﴿No! There is no refuge﴾).

As for His saying: ﴿To your Lord on that day is the place of rest﴾, it is a statement from the side of Allah, exalted is He, addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in this world, as indicated by His saying "on that day." It is therefore a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraq) and an incidental insertion (idmaj, the inclusion of a related point within another discourse) serving to remind of the sovereignty over that day.

In the ascription of (Rabb, "Lord") to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ) there is an allusion that He will be his helper on that day, by exacting retribution from those who did not accept his call.

(al-mustaqarr, "the place of rest") is a noun of place (masdar mimi) from istaqarra, when one settles in a place and does not move, and the sin and ta' are for intensifying the description.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for the sake of restriction (hasr, exclusivity), meaning: to your Lord and not to any other refuge. The meaning is: there is no refuge for the human being on that day except one ending in your Lord. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:28].

The clause (﴿The human being will be informed on that day of what he sent forward and what he left behind﴾) is a resumed statement, in the manner of explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani, a new sentence answering an implicit question raised by the preceding one) prompted by His saying: ﴿To your Lord on that day is the place of rest﴾. (al-mafarr, "the escape"), with a fatha on the mim and a fatha on the fa', is a verbal noun (masdar). The interrogative is used in the sense of wishing (tamanni), meaning: "Would that I had an escape to a place of safety," but he is not able to attain it.

(أيْنَ, "where") is an adverb of place.

(kalla, "no!") is a repudiation and nullification of what was contained in ﴿Where is the escape?﴾ of the hope of finding a way of escape.

[Page 346]

(al-wazar) is the place to which one takes refuge to protect oneself from being struck by something disagreeable, such as mountains and fortresses.

It is possible that ﴿No! There is no refuge﴾ is a new statement from the side of Allah, exalted is He, as an answer to the human being's utterance, meaning: there is no refuge for you. In that case, it is proper to pause at (al-mafarr). It is also possible that it is part of the human being's utterance, meaning: he says, "Where is the escape?" and answers himself by nullifying his hope, saying ﴿No! There is no refuge﴾, meaning: there is no refuge for me. This is by his looking in all directions and finding nothing but the Fire, as is reported in the hadith. In that case, it is good to connect (﴿Where is the escape?﴾) with the clause (﴿No! There is no refuge﴾).

As for His saying: ﴿To your Lord on that day is the place of rest﴾, it is a statement from the side of Allah, exalted is He, addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in this world, as indicated by His saying "on that day." It is therefore a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraq) and an incidental insertion (idmaj, the inclusion of a related point within another discourse) serving to remind of the sovereignty over that day.

In the ascription of (Rabb, "Lord") to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ) there is an allusion that He will be his helper on that day, by exacting retribution from those who did not accept his call.

(al-mustaqarr, "the place of rest") is a noun of place (masdar mimi) from istaqarra, when one settles in a place and does not move, and the sin and ta' are for intensifying the description.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for the sake of restriction (hasr, exclusivity), meaning: to your Lord and not to any other refuge. The meaning is: there is no refuge for the human being on that day except one ending in your Lord. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:28].

The intended meaning of (al-insan, "the human being") should be the disbeliever, in keeping with the context of the preceding verses, because he is the focus of the discourse, although every human being will be informed on that day of what he sent forward and left behind, both the people of good and the people of evil. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the day when every soul will find what it did of good present, and what it did of evil﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:30], and so on. The variation in the contexts of discourse prevents applying the words occurring in them to one single sense, for the Qur'an contains varieties of reminder that do not follow a single method. This is among the matters that some commentators fail to observe when they interpret closely related verses in identical senses.

[Page 347]

Informing the human being of what he sent forward and left behind is a metonymy for recompensing him for what he did: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. It is said to him: "This is the recompense for such-and-such deed," so he knows his deed from that and receives its recompense. Thus the informing is among the necessary consequences of the recompense. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected, then you will surely be informed of what you did﴾ [al-Taghabun 64:7]. In that informing there is reproach and exposure of his condition.

What is meant by (what he sent forward) is what he did, and by (what he left behind) is what he abandoned of what he was commanded to do or forbidden to do, in both states, so that he opposed what he was obligated to, and of what the Prophet (ﷺ) taught as a supplication: "Forgive me what I have sent forward and what I have left behind, what I have concealed and what I have made public."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 75, verses 14–15:

﴿Nay, man will be a witness against himself﴾ ﴿even though he should offer his excuses﴾

This is a transitional turn (idrab intiqali), moving from the content of ﴿Man will be informed on that Day of what he sent ahead and left behind﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13] to the report that the disbeliever knows what he did, because their tongues, hands and feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do. For he reads his book of deeds and says ﴿Would that I had not been given my record, and had not known my account!﴾ [al-Haqqah: 25], and they say ﴿What is this Book that leaves out nothing small or great but has recorded it?﴾ and they find what they did present [al-Kahf: 49]. God the Exalted also says ﴿Read your record; sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner﴾ [al-Isra': 14].

The structure of His saying ﴿Nay, man will be a witness against himself﴾ is suitable for conveying two meanings:

The first: that (basirah) means one who sees, intensely watchful, so that (basirah) is the predicate of (al-insan). And ﴿against himself﴾ is attached to (basirah), i.e., man is a seer over himself. It is construed with the preposition (ala) because it implies the meaning of watchfulness, which is the meaning of His saying in the other verse ﴿sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner﴾ [al-Isra': 14]. The ta' of (basirah) is for emphasis, like the ta' in 'allamah and nassabah, i.e., man is all-knowing, a seer, strong in knowledge of himself on that Day.

The second meaning: that (basirah) is a second subject, and what is meant by it is the companion of man among the guardian angels, and ﴿against himself﴾ is the predicate of the second subject, placed before it, and the whole sentence is a predicate of (al-insan). In this case (basirah) may mean (basir), i.e., seeing. The ta' is for emphasis as mentioned in the first meaning, and the construction with (ala) is for implying the meaning of watcher, as in the first meaning.

It is possible that (basirah) is an adjective of an elided noun, its estimated form being: a clear proof (hujjah basirah), and (basirah) is then a metaphor for being manifest, as in His saying ﴿He said: You have certainly known that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidences (basa'ir)﴾ [al-Isra': 102]. From this is His saying ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign (mubsirah)﴾ [al-Isra': 59], and the feminine form is due to the feminine gender of the noun it modifies.

This sentence has come to function as a proverb because of its brevity and the abundance of its meanings.

The clause ﴿even though he should offer his excuses﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the subject, which is man, and it is a state more fitting for the meaning of its governing verb to be established when it occurs.

This (law) is a concessive (wasliyyah), as was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿never will be accepted from any of them the earth full of gold even if he should ransom himself by it﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 91] in Surah Ali 'Imran. The meaning: he is a witness against himself even in the state of offering his excuses.

Ilqa' (casting) is meant here as an explicit declaration by way of metaphor, as was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿and they cast to them the word: Indeed, you are liars﴾ [al-Nahl: 86] in Surah al-Nahl.

Ma'adhir is the plural form (ism jam') of ma'dhirah, and it is not a true plural, since the proper plural of ma'dhirah would be ma'adhir. Similar to al-ma'adhir is the saying al-manakir, a collective noun of munkar. From al-Dahhak it is reported that ma'adhir here is the plural of mi'dhar, with a kasrah on the mim, meaning a veil in the dialect of Yemen; the casting is then used in its literal meaning, i.e., letting down. The meaning: the disbeliever on that Day knows his deeds for which he deserved punishment, and he tries to make an excuse, while he knows that he has no excuse, even if he were to set forth all his excuses.

And (ma'adhirahu): a plural defined by addition, indicating generality. ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it.﴾ ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its gathering and its recitation.﴾ ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.﴾ ﴿Then indeed upon Us is its clarification.﴾

This verse came here as an interjection (*i'tiraD*, a parenthetical insertion). The occasion of its revelation is what al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he would move his tongue with it, wanting to memorize it out of fear that it would slip from him, or out of his intense desire to memorize it, and so he encountered hardship from that. God the Exalted then revealed (﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its gathering and its recitation.﴾). He said: its gathering in your breast, then We will recite it. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation. He said: so listen to it and be silent. Then indeed upon Us is that We clarify it with your tongue, that is, that you recite it." [End of quotation.] When this revelation descended in the midst of the surah, for the purpose for which it was sent down, and it was not an independent surah, it was appended to the surah and placed between the verses among which it was revealed.

The pronoun in (*bihi*, "with it") refers to the Qur'an, as is well known in many verses.

His statement (﴿So when We have recited it﴾) means: when Jibril recites it on Our behalf. The recitation is attributed to the pronoun of Majesty by way of *majaz 'aqli* (metaphor in the attribution of an act to its agent in the rational sense, a figure of speech), and the indication is clear.

The meaning of (*fattabi' qur'anahu*, "follow its recitation") is: listen attentively to Our recitation.

The pronoun in (*qur'anahu*, "its recitation") refers to what the pronoun of absence in (﴿Do not move with it﴾) refers to, namely the Qur'an in its nominal sense. Thus the occurrence of this verse in this surah is like the occurrence of (﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64]) in Surat Maryam, and the occurrence of (﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]) amid the rulings on wives in Surat al-Baqarah. They said: this verse was revealed in the midst of Surat al-Qiyamah. This is what there is no disagreement about among the people of hadith and the imams of tafsir (exegesis). Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) reported from al-Qaffal that he said: His statement (﴿Do not move with it your tongue﴾) is not addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), but is addressed to the human being mentioned in His statement (﴿The human being will be informed﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13]). So it applies to the human being at the moment he is informed of the evil of his deeds, and it is said to him: "Read your record." When he begins to read, his tongue stammers, so it is said to him: "Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it, for upon Us, by the judgment of promise or by the judgment of wisdom, is it incumbent that We gather your deeds and recite them to you. So when We have recited it to you, follow its recitation by acknowledging it. Then upon Us is the explanation of the degrees of its punishment." Al-Qaffal said: "This is a good interpretation, and there is nothing in reason that rejects it, even though the transmitted reports do not come with it." [End of quotation.]

I say: even if reason does not reject it, the Arabic style and the meanings of the words recoil from it.

What appears to me regarding the placement of this verse here, rather than in the surahs revealed before this one, is this: when the surahs of the Qur'an were few, the Prophet (ﷺ) did not fear that some verses would slip from him. But when the surahs became numerous, reaching about thirty according to what Sa'id ibn Jubayr counted in the order of the revelation of the surahs, the Prophet (ﷺ) began to fear that he would forget some of their verses. So perhaps he (ﷺ) began to move his tongue with the words of the Qur'an when it was revealed, as a precaution for memorizing it, out of his eagerness to convey what was revealed to him in its exact wording. When God undertook to preserve it, He commanded him not to burden himself by moving his tongue. Thus the prohibition against moving his tongue is a prohibition of mercy and compassion, because of the hardship he encountered in that.

The word (*qur'an*) in both places is a verbal noun meaning "recitation," like *al-ghufran* and *al-furqan*. Hassan (ibn Thabit) said in lamenting 'Uthman ibn 'Affan:

"He cuts the night with glorification and recitation of the Qur'an."

The word (*'alayna*, "upon Us") in both places denotes undertaking and guarantee.

The (*thumma*, "then") in (﴿Then indeed upon Us is its clarification﴾) denotes sequence in rank, that is, the difference between the rank of the clause to which it is conjoined, which is His statement (﴿Indeed, upon Us is its gathering and its recitation﴾), and the rank of the conjoined clause, which is (﴿Indeed, upon Us is its clarification﴾). The meaning of the two clauses is: upon Us is the gathering of the revelation and its recitation, and beyond that, that you clarify it to people with your tongue. That is, We undertake on your behalf that its gathering and its recitation be through your tongue, that is, from your memory, not by a writing that you read, but that it be preserved in the breasts, clear to every hearer, not depending on consultation or on bringing a *mushaf* (written copy of the Qur'an) from near or far.

Thus the clarification here is the clarification of its words, not the clarification of its meanings, because the clarification of its meanings is necessarily connected to the occurrence of its words.

Some of our scholars, who hold the permissibility of delaying the clarification (*bayan*) past the time of the matter needing clarification, have argued from this verse, holding that (*thumma*) denotes sequence. This is a weak argument, because the sequence that (*thumma*) conveys is a sequence in rank, not in time. Moreover, (*thumma*) conjoined the whole clause and did not conjoin the word (*bayanahu*) alone. So if the verse were to be used as an argument, it would necessarily follow that delaying the clarification is a established truth from which clarification is never free, and that is not correct.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 75, verses 20–22:

( ﴿Nay, but you love the hasty life,﴾ ﴿and leave the Hereafter.﴾

This is a return to the principal theme on which the surah is built, just as a speaker returns to connect his speech after it has been interrupted by an incidental matter or a questioner. The word (كَلّا, kallā, "nay") is a rebuke and a nullification. It may be a nullification of what preceded from His words (﴿Does man reckon that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3]) up to His words (﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 15]), so (kallā) is repeated as an emphasis of its counterpart and as a linking of the speech by repeating the last word of it.

The meaning: their claims are false.

His words (بَلْ يُحِبُّونَ العاجِلَةَ, "but you love the hasty life") are a nullifying transition (idrāb ibtālī) that elaborates what the rebuke with (kallā) had summarized of the nullification and refutation of what came before it; that is, they have no genuine excuses in reality, but they love the hasty life (al-'ājilah), i.e., the desires of this world, and leave the Hereafter. The speech implies reproach, and the basis of the reproach is loving the hasty life together with rejecting the Hereafter. As for one who loves the hasty life but also attends to the Hereafter, i.e., conforms to the legislated commands and prohibitions, he is not blameworthy. He, the Exalted, said, reporting about those among the people of Qarun who had been given knowledge (﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77]).

It may also be a nullification of what was contained in His words (﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 15]), in which case it is an independent new statement (istiʾnaf ibtidāʾī). The meaning: their excuses are false, but they love the hasty life and leave the Hereafter, i.e., they preferred their desires, which are hasty, and did not reckon any reckoning for the Hereafter.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (تُحِبُّونَ, "you love") and (تَذَرُونَ, "you leave") with a feminine-second-person-marked ta' at the start (taʾ fawqiyyah), by iltifat (shift) from the third person to the second person, in admonishing the polytheists directly with the branching-off, since that is more eloquent in it. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a ya' at the start (yāʾ taḥtiyyah), in line with the preceding third-person pronouns, and the pronoun returns to (al-insan, "man") in His words (﴿Nay, man is a witness against himself﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 14]); it came as a plural pronoun because al-insan is meant as the polytheistic people. And in His words (﴿but you love﴾) there is what guides to clarifying the meaning of acquisition (kasb), which Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari was granted success in explaining, namely inclination and love toward an act or its abandonment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 75, verses 23–25:

(﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] ﴿looking toward their Lord﴾ ﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾ ﴿thinking that a calamity is about to befall them﴾)

What is meant by "that Day" (yawma'idhin) is the Day of Resurrection, which has been mentioned in this same manner from the beginning with His words (﴿On that Day man will say, "Where is the escape?"﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 10]) and repeated twice.

The sentence omitted after the particle (idh), for which the tanwin is the substitute, is estimated to be: "on the Day when the sight is dazzled."

From this, there is a transition to a general description of the state of people on the Day of Resurrection, between the people of happiness and the people of misery.

So the radiant faces are the faces of the people of happiness, and the gloomy faces are the faces of the people of misery, and this is clear from both sentences.

The ones intended by the two groups were already known to people from the Qur'an revealed earlier, such as His words in Surat 'Abasa (﴿And faces that Day will have dust upon them, covered with darkness. Those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ ['Abasa: 40–42]). Thus it is known that the root of the causes of happiness is faith in Allah alone, affirming His Messenger ﷺ and believing in what the Messenger ﷺ brought, and that the root of the causes of misery is associating partners with Allah, denying the Messenger ﷺ, and rejecting what he brought. The opening of this surah also contains what points to this, such as His words (﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3]) and His words (﴿Rather, man wants to continue in sin before him﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 5]).

The indefiniteness of (wujuh, "faces") is for variety and division, like His exalted words (﴿A party will be in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7]) and the verse of the poet, which is from the verses of the book al-Adab, whose author did not attribute it, nor did the author of al-'Ubab in his commentary attribute it:

"One day is against us and one day is for us, one day we are tested and one day we are made to triumph."

And the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

"One day with cavalry you drive the Romans away from them, and one day with generosity you drive away poverty and drought."

So the radiant faces, described by radiance (nadrah, with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the dad), which is the beauty of the face from the effect of blessing and joy; its verb is like nasara, karuma and farihа, and hence it is said: nadir, nadir and nadir. Radiance of the faces is a metonymy for the joy of their owners and their bliss. Allah said of the people of happiness (﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 24]), because what arises in the soul of emotions shows its effect.

He informed about them with a second predicate in His words (﴿looking toward their Lord﴾). The apparent meaning of the word (nazirah) is that it derives from nazara in the sense of seeing with the eye, declaring the honour of those faces: that they look toward the side of Allah, exalted is He, with a special look in which no one of lower rank shares. This is the general meaning of the verse, established by the apparent wording of the Qur'an, and authentic reports from the Prophet ﷺ have confirmed it.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayrah that "some people said: O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection? He said: Do you suffer any difficulty in seeing the sun and the moon when they are clear? We said: No. He said: You will not suffer any difficulty in seeing your Lord on that Day, except as you suffer in seeing them."

In another narration: "Indeed you will see Him in this manner," and he related the hadith concerning intercession.

Al-Bukhari related from Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "We were sitting with the Prophet ﷺ when he looked at the moon on the night of the full moon and said: Indeed you will see your Lord just as you see this moon, you will not be harmed in seeing it, and perhaps he said: 'You will see your Lord with your own eyes.'"

Muslim related from Suhayb ibn Sinan, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, Allah, exalted is He, says: Do you want anything more that I should give you? They say: Did You not whiten our faces? Did You not admit us into Paradise and save us from the Fire? He said: Then He lifts the veil, and they are not given anything more beloved to them than looking at their Lord."

The indication of the verse that the believers see with their eyes a sight related to the Essence of Allah, in general terms, is an implicit indication, because it admits interpretations. The Mu'tazilah interpreted it to mean the sight of His majesty and the splendour of His holiness, which is not granted to anyone other than the people of happiness.

This is linked to the ambiguous attributes, even though its implication is not the affirmation of an attribute; yet it leads to an attribute and entails it, because it amounts to the attribution of a direction to the Essence and a measure that is encompassed in whole or in part, if the sight is with the eye. Therefore the promise of the people of Paradise seeing their Lord, exalted is He, is rightly counted among the ambiguous matters.

The scholars of Islam have differing understandings of this. As for the early generation of the community and its predecessors, they followed the path they had acquired in the conduct of the Prophet ﷺ: believing in what came of this kind in its general sense, and turning their attention away from delving into determining its reality and placing it under one of the divisions of rational judgment. They heard this and its like, all of it or some of it or a little of it, but they did not occupy themselves with it nor did they seek its detailed explanation; rather they turned to what was more deserving of attention, namely striving to establish the Shari'ah, spread it and secure its authority, while firmly affirming the transcendence of Allah, exalted is He, above the necessary consequences attached to the apparent meanings of those attributes. Their imam to whom they referred in all of this was His saying, exalted is He (﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]), or what is close to it of the specific proofs of transcendence, such as His saying (﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103]), with respect to our present station, while they agreed that not knowing the details of this does not harm the creed of faith. But when the seeking of knowing the realities of things arose among the scholars of Islam, and scholarly research compelled them to delve into the meanings of the Qur'an, the subtleties of its expressions and the particularities of its eloquence, they did not find the method of the predecessors convincing to the minds of the scholars of later generations, because their method in knowledge was a method of scrutiny, which suited their age. Compare with this what arose among the sects of the Muslim community of doctrinal schools, and the casting of the doubts of the heretics, from those who ascribed themselves to Islam and others, which prompted them to probe deeply and to establish knowledge on pillars that do not accept shaking, and to repel the doubts of the skeptics and refute the attacks of the heretics. So they followed paths of reconciling contradictory statements and meanings, and affirming each truth in its proper place, by way of interpretation that the context requires and that evidence supports.

So some groups followed the path of general interpretation, by believing in those ambiguous matters in their general form, being certain of God's transcendence above their apparent meanings, but without separating their turning away from their apparent meanings in detail; rather they keep the interpretation general. This group is called the Salafiyyah, because their method is close to the method of the predecessors regarding ambiguous matters. These groups differ in the extent to which they rooted their principles, a difference that made them into sects. Among them are the Hanabilah, the Zahiriyyah, and the ancient Kharijites, other than those who adopted the method of the Mu'tazilah.

Among them are the Ahl al-Sunnah who existed before al-Ash'ari, such as the Malikiyyah and the people of hadith who held fast to the apparent meanings of the sound reports from the Prophet ﷺ, with the qualification that they are interpreted away from their apparent meanings in a general way. Some of those who adopted the apparent meaning went to extremes, such as the Karramiyyah and the Mushabbihah, and they were grouped with the first category.

Among them are the sects of the theologians who sought to reconcile the rules of rational sciences with what the statements of the Book and the Sunnah brought, and these are the Mu'tazilah, the Ash'ariyyah, and the Maturidiyyah.

Their views on the sight of the people of Paradise of their Lord are woven on this pattern:

The early generation affirmed it without inquiry; the Mu'tazilah denied it and interpreted the evidences by means such as metaphor, homonymy, and supposing an omitted element, because it contradicts the definitive principles according to them; so they preferred what they saw as definitive and discarded the evidences.

The Ash'ariyyah affirmed it and sought to establish it with proofs that yield certainty and refute the Mu'tazilah's view, but they did not reach the desired goal in this.

What each group brought of arguments was not free from objections, refutations and counter-arguments; and likewise what each group raised against its opponents of counter-arguments was not free from bare objections or objections accompanied by their supporting premises. So the taking and rejecting prolonged, and no benefit was achieved, nor was a final conclusion reached.

It is good that we entrust its modality to the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, as with the rest of the ambiguous matters that relate to the affairs of the Creator, exalted is He.

This is the meaning of the saying of our predecessors that it is a sight "without modality" (bila kayf), and it is a comprehensive true word, even if the Mu'tazilah recoil from it.

This is what relates to the indication of the verse regarding the sight of the people of Paradise of their Lord. ﴿Nay, when it reaches the collarbones﴾ ﴿and it is said, "Who can cure him?"﴾ ﴿and he thinks it is the parting﴾ ﴿and leg is wound about leg﴾ ﴿to your Lord, that Day, is the driving.﴾

This is a second *radʿ* (a rebuke or repudiation, a "nay") directed at the human's saying (﴿When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ [75:6]). It reinforces the earlier *radʿ* in His saying (﴿Nay, but you love the hasty life﴾ [75:20]). Its meaning is a rebuke against denying the resurrection, for it is an event that is not far off. Every person witnesses it at the time of death's approach, as His saying indicates: (﴿to your Lord, that Day, is the driving﴾). The description of the signs of the Resurrection's immediate arrival is followed by a description of the signs of the arrival of the first preparation for meeting Him, when one departs from the first life.

It is related from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba that they say, "The Resurrection, the Resurrection," but the resurrection of each of them is his death. And it is related from 'Alqama that he attended a funeral, and when the deceased was buried he said, "As for this one, his resurrection has taken place." So the state of approaching death is the last of the states of the worldly life, followed by the soul's passage into the direct disposal of God, exalted is He.

It is also a rebuke against preferring this world over the Hereafter, as if it were said: "Be restrained and take heed of what lies before you of death, at which the hasty life ends and you are transferred to the deferred life." Thus it is a rebuke against loving the hasty life and abandoning concern for the Hereafter. It is not, therefore, a reinforcement of the *radʿ* in His saying (﴿Nay, but you love the hasty life﴾ [75:20]); rather, it is a rebuke of what that earlier rebuke contained, namely preferring the hasty life over the Hereafter.

The phrase (﴿when it reaches the collarbones﴾) is linked to the complement that is to be supposed in the predicate, which is His saying (to your Lord). The meaning: the driving will be to your Lord when it reaches the collarbones.

The clause (﴿to your Lord, that Day, is the driving﴾) explains the rebuke and brings closer the refutation of the disbelief attributed to the deniers of resurrection in His saying (﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾ [75:6]).

(*Idhā*) is an adverb that carries the sense of a condition, and it is in the accusative governed by its answer, namely His saying (﴿to your Lord, that Day, is the driving﴾).

The fronting of (to your Lord) before what it modifies, which is (the driving), serves to give it emphasis, because it is the focus of their denial.

The pronoun in (reaches) refers to something not mentioned in the speech, but it is known from the verb (reaches) and from the mention of (the collarbones), for the verb (﴿reaches the collarbones﴾) indicates that what is meant is the human's soul. The implied meaning is: when the soul or the self reaches. This supposition is indicated by the verb that is attributed to the pronoun, according to the usage of the speakers of the language. A similar example is the verse of Hatim al-Ta'i:

*O my two companions, wealth does not avail a man*
*when the throat rattles one day and the chest constricts over it.*

That is: when the self rattles. From this same usage is the Arabs' saying "*arsalat*" (she sent), meaning "the sky sent the rain." It is also permissible to supply in the verse what the actual situation indicates.

[Page 358]

The (*anfās*) is the plural of *nafas* with a fatḥa on the fā', and it is more suitable to the realities.

The (*tarāqī*) is the plural of *tarqūwa* (collarbone), with a fatḥa on the tā', a sukūn on the rā', a ḍamma on the qāf, a fatḥa on the wāw (lightened), and the feminine ending. It is the hollow of the throat, and every human has two collarbones, one on his right and one on his left.

So the plural is used here in place of the dual, for the purpose of lightening the wording, and there is no ambiguity. This is because the dual of *tarqūwa* carries some heaviness that is not suitable to the most eloquent speech. This is like what occurs in His saying (﴿Your hearts have inclined﴾ [66:4]) in surah al-Tahrim.

The meaning of (﴿reaches the collarbones﴾) is that the soul has reached the windpipe, where the final breaths exit, so that their sound is heard only in the direction of the collarbone. This is the last stage of the state of dying. Similar is His saying, exalted is He (﴿Why then, when it reaches the throat﴾ [56:83]), and so on.

The *lām* in (*tarāqī*) is like the *lām* in (*masāq*). It is said that it is a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning: his soul reached his collarbones, i.e., the human's collarbones.

Some exegetes interpreted saddaqa as "gave charity" (a'ta al-sadaqa), but this does not follow the morphological pattern, since its proper form would be tasaddaqa. The clause ﴿nor prayed﴾ is joined to the negation of affirming, to disparage him by showing that his condition is opposed to the conditions of the people of Islam. The meaning is: he neither believed nor submitted.

This is the meaning of al-Kisa'i's statement: "la" is used in the sense of "lam" (not), but it is conjoined with another negation. The Arabs say: "Neither 'Abd Allah is going out nor so-and-so," and they do not say: "I passed by a man who is not kind" until it is said: "nor generous." When no other negation is conjoined to it, a past verb does not follow "la" except when a supplication is intended, as in "may your mouth not be broken." Anything that departs from this is anomalous.

As for His words: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [90:11], it is interpreted as repeating the negation, because the object of the verb negated by "la" is "the steep path," which includes several negated matters, explained by His words: ﴿And what can make you know what the steep path is? Since this is the object of the negated verb, the verb is taken as repeating the negation, as if it were said: "He did not free a slave, nor feed an orphan, nor feed a needy man, nor believe."

This is either merely to emphasize the meaning by mentioning its opposite, as in His words: ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you did by mistake, but what your hearts intended﴾ [33:5], or to clarify a general statement in the preceding negation, as in: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men, but he is the Messenger of God﴾ [33:40].

The lightly pronounced "lakin" does not govern case endings (i'rab), so it is a particle of beginning (harf ibtida'), and for this reason it most often occurs after the conjunction "wa" (and). The clause ﴿but he denied and turned away﴾ conveys two meanings: first, that "denied" emphasizes His words ﴿So he did not believe﴾; second, that it clarifies the meaning of ﴿So he did not believe﴾ by showing that he turned away deliberately, since lack of belief has several states. It has been said that His words ﴿So woe to them﴾ [47:20], from His words ﴿So woe to them, obedience and honorable speech﴾ [47:20–21] in the Surah of Muhammad, are of this kind, according to one interpretation, which makes ﴿obedience and honorable speech﴾ a new independent clause and not the agent of the elative form. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi held that "awla" is a proper name for the meaning of "woe" (al-wayl), and that its pattern is "af'al" from "wayl," which is destruction. So its original morphology was "awyal lak," meaning "more destructive for you." Then transposition (qalb) occurred to seek lightness: the ya' was moved to the end of the word, and it became "awla" in the pattern of "aflah." When the weak letter was vowelled and the letter before it was opened, it was changed into an alif, so they said "awla" in the form of "fa'la."

The kaf (you) is a second-person address to the man, who was explicitly mentioned several times in the preceding verses by way of the third person, both as noun and pronoun. Here He shifted from the third-person form to the second-person address by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), in order to confront the man with the supplication, because confrontation is more effective in rebuke. The apparent expectation would have been "awla lahu."

His words ﴿fa-awla﴾ are an emphasis of ﴿awla lak﴾, and the fa' of consequence is used in it to show that a supplication is being made against him that harm should follow him, and that it should be followed by another supplication.

Qatada said: The Messenger of God ﷺ came out of the mosque and met Abu Jahl at the gate of the Banu Makhzum. The Messenger of God took hold of Abu Jahl by his clothes and said to him: "Woe to you, and woe again; woe to you, and woe again." Abu Jahl said: "Muhammad threatens me," meaning he uses the word of supplication to mean a threat. "By God, I am the most mighty of the people of the valley." God then revealed: ﴿Woe to you, and woe again﴾, as He had said to Abu Jahl.

His words ﴿Then woe to you, and woe again﴾ are an emphasis of the supplication against him and of his preceding emphasis.

This is a continuation (tafri') based on His words: ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾ [75:6].

The pronoun refers to "man" (al-insan) in His words: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [75:3], meaning that because he denied resurrection, he did not prepare for it.

The object of "denied" (kadhdhaba) is omitted so that it includes everything the polytheists denied. The implied meaning is: he denied the Messenger, the Qur'an, and resurrection, and he turned away from accepting the laws of Islam.

This appears in His words: ﴿When the earth is pounded to powder, and your Lord comes and the angels in rows, and Hell is brought that Day—that Day man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him? He will say, "Oh, would that I had sent forth for my life!"﴾ [89:21–24].

The verb "believed" (saddaqa) is derived from tasdiq (affirming), meaning affirming the Messenger ﷺ and the Qur'an, and this is what suits His words: ﴿but he denied﴾.

The meaning is: he did not believe in what the Messenger ﷺ brought. Some exegetes interpreted saddaqa as "gave charity" (a'ta al-sadaqa), but this does not follow the morphological pattern, since its proper form would be tasaddaqa. Moreover, it does not fit the adversative (istidrak) in His words: ﴿but he denied﴾.

The clause ﴿nor prayed﴾ is joined to the negation of affirming, to disparage him by showing that his condition is opposed to the conditions of the people of Islam. The meaning is: he neither believed nor submitted.

The particle "la" (not) is negating a past verb. It is most common, when negating a past verb, for another negation to be conjoined to it, and that happens when the speaker intends two matters, as here and in the verse of Zuhayr:

*Nor did he conceal it, nor did he advance.*

This is the meaning of al-Kisa'i's statement: "la" is used in the sense of "lam" (not), but it is conjoined with another negation. The Arabs say: "Neither 'Abd Allah is going out nor so-and-so," and they do not say: "I passed by a man who is not kind" until it is said: "nor generous." When no other negation is conjoined to it, a past verb does not follow "la" except when a supplication is intended, as in "may your mouth not be broken." Anything that departs from this is anomalous.

As for His words: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [90:11], it is interpreted as repeating the negation, because the object of the verb negated by "la" is "the steep path," which includes several negated matters, explained by His words: ﴿And what can make you know what the steep path is? Freeing a slave, or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan of near relation or a needy man in misery, then being of those who believed﴾ [90:12–17]. Since this is the object of the negated verb, the verb is taken as repeating the negation, as if it were said: "He did not free a slave, nor feed an orphan, nor feed a needy man, nor believe."

The clause ﴿but he denied﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿So he did not believe﴾.

The particle "lakin" (but), when lightly pronounced (lakin al-mukhaffaf), is originally a particle of adversative (istidrak), that is, of correcting part of what the preceding sentence contained. This is either merely to emphasize the meaning by mentioning its opposite, as in His words: ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you did by mistake, but what your hearts intended﴾ [33:5], or to clarify a general statement in the preceding negation, as in: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men, but he is the Messenger of God﴾ [33:40].

The lightly pronounced "lakin" does not govern case endings (i'rab), so it is a particle of beginning (harf ibtida'), and for this reason it most often occurs after the conjunction "wa" (and). The clause ﴿but he denied and turned away﴾ conveys two meanings: first, that "denied" emphasizes His words ﴿So he did not believe﴾; second, that it clarifies the meaning of ﴿So he did not believe﴾ by showing that he turned away deliberately, since lack of belief has several states. A parallel outside the adversative context is His words: ﴿Except Iblis, who refused and was arrogant﴾ [2:34].

"Denial" (al-takdhib) is denying resurrection, the Qur'an, and the mission of Muhammad ﷺ.

"Turning away" (al-tawalli) is turning away from his call to reflect and ponder over the Qur'an.

The subject of "believed" and the verbs mentioned after it are pronouns referring to the man previously mentioned.

"Yatamattha" means he walks with a swagger, with the mim vowelled with a damma, the ta' with a fatha followed by a ya' and then a ta' (ṭ), whether shortened or lengthened. It means strutting.

The root of "yatamatta" is "yatamaṭṭaṭu," meaning he stretches himself out, because the one who struts stretches his steps, and this is the gait of one who is self-admiring. Here the description of the denying man ends.

The meaning is: he neglected preparation for the Hereafter and paid no attention to the call of the Messenger ﷺ, and went to his family proud of himself, not reflecting on his destiny.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Most of those who interpreted (the Qur'an) said that this whole passage, from His words ﴿So he did not believe nor pray﴾,
