﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that resumes the discourse). The speech returns to arguing for the possibility of resurrection, which was where it began. It is linked to ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3], as though it were said: Does he think that We will not assemble his bones, and does he think that We will leave him in a state of non-existence?

It adds here that the requirement of divine wisdom (*hikmah*) is that man should not be left neglected, as you will come to know.

The interrogative is a denial (*istifham inkari*), like the one that preceded it in the Almighty's words ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3].

The original meaning of *tark* (leaving) is one thing separating from another by the choice of the one who leaves. It is used figuratively for a person neglecting something and not caring for its affairs or attending to it. Here it is used in the figurative sense.

The meaning of what man is left upon here is what the context indicates, namely the state of non-existence without revival, which is indicated by the Almighty's words ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3] and His words ﴿On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward and put off﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13].

The verb *yutraka* is not constructed with an active subject but with a passive (*yunaib*, the deputy of the agent). This is done for brevity (*ijaz*), since the agent is known from the earlier words ﴿that We will not assemble his bones﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3]. It is as though He said: Does man think that We will leave him without resurrection and that We will neglect his deeds in vain? The mention of *sudan* (in vain) comes here by way of embedding (*idmaj*) within what the speech was directed toward, indicating that the requirement of the wisdom of creating man is that his Creator not leave him after death, so that He does not revive him to repay him for what he did in his first life.

Repeating ﴿Does man think﴾ prepares for what follows of the evidence for the possibility of resurrection from the side of matter, in His words ﴿Was he not a drop of sperm﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 37], to the end of the surah.

So His words ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ are a repetition and enumeration of the denial directed at the disbelievers for their denial of resurrection. Do you not see that it came after the description of the Day of Resurrection and the reckoning in it for what man sent forward and put off?

The meaning of this is like His words ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115].

*Sudan*, with a dammah on the sin and a short vowel, is a noun meaning "the neglected." It is also said *sada* with a fathah on the sin, though the dammah is more common. It is a noun in which the singular and plural are the same. One says *ibil sudan* (camels left unattended) and *jamal sudan* (a camel left unattended). A verb is derived from it, so one says *asda ibilahu* and *asdaytu ibili* (I left my camels unattended), and its alif is converted from a waw.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) did not explain this word, nor did al-Raghib in al-Mufradat (al-Raghib al-Isfahani). *Sudan* occurs in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of the pronoun in *yutraka*.

He who created man in the best of forms, perfected his composition, and bestowed upon him rational faculties that He did not give to any other kind of animal, so that he might use them for benefits that cannot be counted, or for their opposite, grave corruptions, is not fitting in His wisdom to neglect him like an animal, making the righteous like the corrupters and those who obey their Lord like the criminals. He is the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, who, with His wisdom and power, is able to make the final return to Himself. If He neglected him, the people of corruption would triumph in a world of decline, and the righteous would meet nothing from their righteousness but hardship. It does not suit the wisdom of the Wise that people be left wandering in every valley, and their abandonment becomes an example for the proverb "the wind is for the enemy."

For this reason, in the case of the argument for the occurrence of resurrection, He said ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3], that is, that We will not recreate him and raise him for recompense as We have informed them. In the matter of His wisdom, He came with something resembling the previous style, saying ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾, with the added benefit of what the clause ﴿that he will be left neglected﴾ indicates, namely that he does not think he will be left unregarded by the obligation (*taklif*), as camels are left. That requires recompense.

From al-Shafi'i: "The people of knowledge of the Qur'an have not differed, as far as I know, that *sudan* is that which is neither commanded nor forbidden." End of quotation.

It has become clear from this that His words ﴿that he will be left neglected﴾ are an allusion (*kinayah*) to recompense, because obligation in the present life is intended to lead to recompense in the Hereafter.

[Page 367]

This is a resumption (istinaf) that serves as the cause and clarification of the rebuttal introduced by His words ﴿Does man think he will be left aimless?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:36]. That verse is repeated and confirmed in its meaning by His words ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:3]. The meaning is: the creation of man from a weak substance, and his gradual development through the stages of his existence, is evidence of God's power to bring him into being a second time after his parts have scattered and decayed. The sense of the speech therefore connects as follows: "Does man think that We will not assemble his bones and consider that impossible? Did We not begin his creation when We formed him as a drop of semen, then his creation developed through stages? So what would make it impossible for Us to recreate him a second time in the same way?" God, the Exalted, said: ﴿As We began the first creation, so We will return it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:104].

These sentences are a preparation for His words ﴿Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?﴾

This explanation applies to one of the two meanings of "left" (tarak) in the verse, namely being left without being brought back to life. I will suffice with this explanation rather than explaining the other meaning, which is restricted by His words "aimless" (sudan), that is, being left without recompense for one's deeds, since the benefit of resurrection is that one is repaid for one's action. The meaning is: "Does he think he will be left to perish without his life being renewed?"

The description "aimless" falls within this passage in the position of evidence for the necessity of raising people from the standpoint of wisdom, and after it the discourse moves to showing the possibility of resurrection from the standpoint of substance. Thus its occurrence is an inclusion (idmaj).

Man was created from water and developed through stages until he became a living body of complete form and sensation. Some of him became of the male kind and some of the female kind. The One who was able to create this wondrous creation is not incapable of recreating each one as He created him the first time, with precise wisdom and by another method known only to Him.

The nutfah (drop) is a small quantity of water, and the term was applied to reproductive fluid. This was discussed in Surat Fatir.

Scholars differed on the meaning of ﴿tumna﴾ (poured out). Many commentators said it means "shed." No lexicon records that the verb manā or amnā is used in the sense of "shed," except that some lexicographers, in explaining the name Mina in Makkah, said it was so named because the blood of sacrificial animals is shed there. They did not clarify whether it is an unaugmented verb or has the causative hamza.

I consider this one of the well-known contrivances of lexicographers, who sought a root for the derivation of proper names, and it is clearly forced. The name Mina is a proper noun coined as such. Tha'lab said it was named after the saying "God decreed death for him" (manā Allahu 'alayhi al-mawt), meaning He decreed it, because sacrificial animals are slaughtered there. Ibn Shumayl and Ibn 'Uyaynah said the same. Some commentators explained ﴿tumna﴾ as "created," from the expression "God manā the creation," meaning He created them. The more evident view is that of some commentators that it is the present tense of amnā al-rajul (the man ejaculated), and it is thus like His words ﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:58] in Surat al-Waqi'ah.

The 'alaqah (clot) is a small piece of congealed blood.

The verb ﴿kāna 'alaqah﴾ is joined by the particle thumma (then) to indicate a rank-based delay, since his being a clot is more remarkable than his being a drop, because he became a clot after being water, mixing with what the female womb secretes of ova, and from the combination of the two came a clot. This is as discussed in the purpose of the qualification in His words in Surat al-Najm: ﴿from a drop when it is emitted﴾ [al-Najm 53:46].

Since his formation as a clot is the beginning of the creation of the body, the phrase ﴿fa-khalaqa﴾ (then He created) is joined to it with fa (so), because the clot is followed by becoming a lump of flesh (mudghah), until the body's creation is completed and the soul is breathed into it.

The pronoun in ﴿khalaqa﴾ refers to ﴿Rabbika﴾ (your Lord). Likewise ﴿fa-sawwa﴾ (then proportioned) is joined with fa.

Taswiyah means making a thing equal, that is, balanced and well formed. God said: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:29], and ﴿He who created and proportioned﴾ [al-A'la 87:2]. That is, He made him a body of bone and flesh.

The objects of ﴿khalaqa﴾ and ﴿sawwa﴾ are both omitted, since the context indicates them: that is, ﴿fa-khalaqahu fa-sawwahu﴾ (so He created him and proportioned him).

This is followed by His creating him as male or female, as a pair, and from these two reproduction also occurs.

The majority of readers recited ﴿tumna﴾ with the feminine ending (tumnā, with taa' above) as an attribute of ﴿nutfah﴾. Hafs and Ya'qub recited it with the yaa' below (yumnā) as an attribute of ﴿maniyy﴾.

The sentence ﴿Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?﴾ stands in the position of the conclusion from the evidence, because the creation of a human body from nothing, which is established by direct observation, is more deserving of being deemed unlikely than returning life to the body after death, whether the body remains intact or some or most of it has decayed. Breathing life into it and restoring what has perished of its parts is closer than bringing the body into being from nothing.

The interrogation is a denial of the negated, in the manner of an affirmative denial, and this is the common use of the affirmative interrogative: it falls upon the negation of what is intended to be affirmed, so that this becomes like an expansion upon what is established, if the intent is denial, as a metonymy for the speaker's confidence that the addressee cannot deny it.

In this conclusion there is the rhetorical embellishment of radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr (returning the end to the beginning), since the surah opened with a denial that the polytheists should reckon the resurrection impossible. The discourse on this matter proceeded through various forms of affirmation, threat, conditional statement and argument, until it led to the conclusion that God is able to give life to the dead. This is the aim that was introduced in His words: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:3] ﴿Yes, We are able to restore even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:4].

The generalization of ﴿the dead﴾ in His words ﴿Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?﴾, after the discourse had been directed at the specific disbelieving human or a specific disbeliever, makes the sentence ﴿Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?﴾ a concluding summation (tadhyil).

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surat al-Insan

It was called in the time of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) "Surat Hal Ata 'ala al-Insan" (the surah of "Has there come upon man").

al-Bukhari narrated in the chapter on recitation at Fajr in his Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite at Fajr: 'Alif Lam Mim, the Prostration' and 'Has there come upon man'."

The author of al-Itqan limited himself to naming this surah "Surat al-Insan" when mentioning the Meccan and Medinan surahs, and he did not mention it among the surahs that have more than one name.

It is called "Surat al-Dahr" in many copies of the Qur'an.

al-Khafaji said it is called "Surat al-Amshaj," because the word al-amshaj occurs in it and does not occur in any other part of the Qur'an.

al-Tabarsi mentioned that it is called "Surat al-Abrar," because it contains a description of the delights of the righteous (al-abrar), and they are mentioned by this term there. I have not seen it, since it has changed.

[Page 370]

These are five names for this surah.

Scholars differed about it: it was said to be Meccan, it was said to be Medinan, and it was said that some of it is Meccan and some Medinan. From Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Talhah, Qatadah and Muqatil: it is Meccan, and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, because he so arranged it in his codex, as narrated by Abu Dawud, as will come shortly. On this view most tafsir works rely, and al-Khafaji attributed it to the majority.

Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is Medinan, and this is the view of Jabir ibn Zayd, and it is also reported from Qatadah. al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and al-Kalbi said: it is Medinan except His words ﴿So be patient for the decision of your Lord, and do not obey from among them any sinner or ungrateful one﴾ [al-Insan 76:24] to the end of it, or His words ﴿So be patient for the decision of your Lord, and do not obey from among them﴾ [al-Insan 76:24], etc. These did not mention which surah those verses belonged to that were counted in Mecca until Surat al-Insan was revealed in Medina, and this is strange. They also did not specify in which surah it was recited.

The more correct view is that it is Meccan, since its style and meanings follow the patterns of the Meccan surahs. I do not think the reason for counting it as Medinan is anything other than what is reported: that the verse ﴿They feed the food, despite their love for it﴾ [al-Insan 76:8] was revealed about 'Ali ibn Abi Talib feeding a poor man one night in Medina, an orphan another night, and a captive another night, and the Muslims had no captives in Mecca, by understanding the word "captive" to mean a prisoner of war. Or it is what is reported: that it was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah, who was an Ansari. Often they ascribed the revelation of a verse to examples whose meanings apply to it, and so they expressed these as occasions of revelation, as I explained in the Fifth Introduction.

Jabir ibn Zayd counted it as the ninety-eighth in the order of revelation of the surahs, and said: it was revealed after Surat al-Rahman and before Surat al-Talaq. This follows his view that it is Medinan.

If the more correct view is that it is Meccan, following the arrangement of the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, then it would be the thirtieth or thirty-first, and it would be worthy of being counted before Surat al-Qiyamah or thereabouts, as stated in Ibn Mas'ud's arrangement.

Abu Dawud narrated in the chapter on dividing the Qur'an into parts (tahzib) in his Sunan, from 'Alqamah and al-Aswad, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite the similar surahs (al-nazha'ir), the two surahs," and he counted surahs, saying: "Has there come upon man" and "I swear by the Day of Resurrection" [al-Qiyamah 75:1] in one rak'ah. This is as discussed in the purpose of the qualification in His words in Surat al-Najm: ﴿from a drop when it is emitted﴾ [al-Najm 53:46].

Since his formation as a clot is the beginning of the creation of the body, the phrase ﴿fa-khalaqa﴾ (then He created) is joined to it with fa (so), because the clot is followed by becoming a lump of flesh (mudghah), until the body's creation is completed and the soul is breathed into it.

The pronoun in ﴿khalaqa﴾ refers to ﴿Rabbika﴾ (your Lord). Likewise ﴿fa-sawwa﴾ (then proportioned) is joined with fa.

Taswiyah means making a thing equal, that is, balanced and well formed. God said: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:29], and ﴿He who created and proportioned﴾ [al-A'la 87:2]. That is, He made him a body of bone and flesh.

The objects of ﴿khalaqa﴾ and ﴿sawwa﴾ are both omitted, since the context indicates them: that is, ﴿fa-khalaqahu fa-sawwahu﴾ (so He created him and proportioned him).

This is followed by His creating him as male or female, as a pair, and from these two reproduction also occurs.

The majority of readers recited ﴿tumna﴾ with the feminine ending (tumnā, with taa' above) as an attribute of ﴿nutfah﴾. Hafs and Ya'qub recited it with the yaa' below (yumnā) as an attribute of ﴿maniyy﴾.

The sentence ﴿Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?﴾ stands in the position of the conclusion from the evidence, because the creation of a human body from nothing, which is established by direct observation, is more deserving of being deemed unlikely than returning life to the body after death, whether the body remains intact or some or most of it has decayed. Breathing life into it and restoring what has perished of its parts is closer than bringing the body into being from nothing.

The interrogation is a denial of the negated, in the manner of an affirmative denial, and this is the common use of the affirmative interrogative: it falls upon the negation of what is intended to be affirmed, so that this becomes like an expansion upon what is established, if the intent is denial, as a metonymy for the speaker's confidence that the addressee cannot deny it.

In this conclusion there is the rhetorical embellishment of radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr (returning the end to the beginning), since the surah opened with a denial that the polytheists should reckon the resurrection impossible. The discourse on this matter proceeded through various forms of affirmation, threat, conditional statement and argument, until it led to the conclusion that God is able to give life to the dead. This is the aim that was introduced in His words: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:3] ﴿Yes, We are able to restore even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:4].

The generalization of ﴿the dead﴾ in His words ﴿Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?﴾, after the discourse had been directed at the specific disbelieving human or a specific disbeliever, makes the sentence ﴿Is not He who does that able to give life to the dead?﴾ a concluding summation (tadhyil).

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surat al-Insan

It was called in the time of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) "Surat Hal Ata 'ala al-Insan" (the surah of "Has there come upon man").

al-Bukhari narrated in the chapter on recitation at Fajr in his Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite at Fajr: 'Alif Lam Mim, the Prostration' and 'Has there come upon man'."

The author of al-Itqan limited himself to naming this surah "Surat al-Insan" when mentioning the Meccan and Medinan surahs, and he did not mention it among the surahs that have more than one name.

It is called "Surat al-Dahr" in many copies of the Qur'an.

al-Khafaji said it is called "Surat al-Amshaj," because the word al-amshaj occurs in it and does not occur in any other part of the Qur'an.

al-Tabarsi mentioned that it is called "Surat al-Abrar," because it contains a description of the delights of the righteous (al-abrar), and they are mentioned by this term there. I have not seen it, since it has changed.

[Page 370]

These are five names for this surah.

Scholars differed about it: it was said to be Meccan, it was said to be Medinan, and it was said that some of it is Meccan and some Medinan. From Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Talhah, Qatadah and Muqatil: it is Meccan, and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, because he so arranged it in his codex, as narrated by Abu Dawud, as will come shortly. On this view most tafsir works rely, and al-Khafaji attributed it to the majority.

Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is Medinan, and this is the view of Jabir ibn Zayd, and it is also reported from Qatadah. al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and al-Kalbi said: it is Medinan except His words ﴿So be patient for the decision of your Lord, and do not obey from among them any sinner or ungrateful one﴾ [al-Insan 76:24] to the end of it, or His words ﴿So be patient for the decision of your Lord, and do not obey from among them﴾ [al-Insan 76:24], etc. These did not mention which surah those verses belonged to that were counted in Mecca until Surat al-Insan was revealed in Medina, and this is strange. They also did not specify in which surah it was recited.

The more correct view is that it is Meccan, since its style and meanings follow the patterns of the Meccan surahs. I do not think the reason for counting it as Medinan is anything other than what is reported: that the verse ﴿They feed the food, despite their love for it﴾ [al-Insan 76:8] was revealed about 'Ali ibn Abi Talib feeding a poor man one night in Medina, an orphan another night, and a captive another night, and the Muslims had no captives in Mecca, by understanding the word "captive" to mean a prisoner of war. Or it is what is reported: that it was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah, who was an Ansari. Often they ascribed the revelation of a verse to examples whose meanings apply to it, and so they expressed these as occasions of revelation, as I explained in the Fifth Introduction.

Jabir ibn Zayd counted it as the ninety-eighth in the order of revelation of the surahs, and said: it was revealed after Surat al-Rahman and before Surat al-Talaq. This follows his view that it is Medinan.

If the more correct view is that it is Meccan, following the arrangement of the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, then it would be the thirtieth or thirty-first, and it would be worthy of being counted before Surat al-Qiyamah or thereabouts, as stated in Ibn Mas'ud's arrangement.

Abu Dawud narrated in the chapter on dividing the Qur'an into parts (tahzib) in his Sunan, from 'Alqamah and al-Aswad, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite the similar surahs (al-nazha'ir), the two surahs," and he counted surahs, saying: "Has there come upon man" and "I swear by the Day of Resurrection" [al-Qiyamah 75:1] in one rak'ah. Abu Dawud said: this is the arrangement of Ibn Mas'ud, that is, the arrangement of his codex. And the counters agreed that its verses number thirty-one.

Its purposes

Reminding that every human being was brought into existence after not having been, so how can one judge the impossibility of re-creating him after his non-existence?

And establishing that man is obliged to single out God in worship as thanks to his Creator, and a warning against associating partners with Him.

And establishing recompense for both states, together with some description of that recompense in its two conditions, and elaboration in describing the recompense of the grateful.

Woven into this is the favour bestowed upon people through the blessing of existence and the blessing of perception, and the favour of what man was given of discernment between good and evil and guidance to good through the messengers. Thus among people are those who thanked God's blessing, and among them are those who denied it and worshipped other than Him.

And the strengthening of the Prophet (ﷺ) in bearing the burdens of prophethood and patience with what befalls him in that, and a warning against yielding to the disbelievers, and an indication that being chosen for prophethood is a great blessing which deserves thanks to God by fulfilling what He has chosen him for and by devoting oneself to His worship.

And the command to devote oneself to the remembrance of God and to prayer at times of the day.
